prompt:
You are checking a pull request for a programmer who will read your answer in ten seconds. Compare the evidence below with the pull request's description and the requirement. The reader asks: does this change do what it says, and what did it do that nobody asked for?

Answer with a short check, not a report:
- At most 10 statements in all: matches at most 2, not-in-description at most 4, described-not-found at most 2, left-to-you at most 3. Fewer is better; a heading with nothing to say gets no statement.
- `text` is one line of at most 12 words in a C# developer's terms (unhandled exception, diagnostic no longer reported, public API added). No preamble, no hedging, no restating the description.
- Group related evidence: the same behaviour at several sites, or several items of one kind, is ONE statement that cites all of them. Never write one statement per difference when they say the same thing.
- `detail` is optional: one or two sentences shown only when the reader asks for more. Leave it out when `text` says it all.
- not-in-description is for behaviour or surface the description and requirement do not ask for. Put the largest first. Do not list that the description is short, or documentation and test files that merely accompany the change.
- left-to-you names a decision only the reviewer can make, as a question, citing its q<n> items; questions about the same thing share one statement.
- `summaries` gives each heading that has statements one line of at most 12 words that stands for all of them.
- State only what the evidence below shows. You have not seen the code: name no method, call, cast, operator or mechanism that does not appear in this prompt, in `text`, `detail` or `summaries`, and do not guess how the change was made.
Every statement cites item IDs from this prompt (d<n>, b<n>, q<n>, test names, test categories, preset:d<n>, reproduction, File.cs:line). A statement citing anything else is discarded. Never use the words proved, safe, verified, trusted, correct.
